message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure proposal

**Overall:** The direction is plausible, since the hotel is priced below its competitive set and has sold out 31 Saturdays. But the central claim, that the evidence shows guests are not price sensitive, is not supported. The headline revenue figure has an error and is described incorrectly, and the two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business the document itself identifies. I would not approve it in its current form.

## Major issues

**1. The price-sensitivity evidence is confounded (Section 3)**
- The comparison is June 81% to July 89% after a £10 rise. But Section 2 says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal lift explains the jump without any pricing effect.
- The rise came in the last week of June, so June is almost entirely a pre-rise month. There is no control, such as July 2024 vs July 2025, or movement in the comp set over the same period.
- The test was £10 (about 7%). The proposal is £20 (about 14%), and the document extrapolates from one to the other.
- "Reinforced our positioning as a quality option" is speculation.
- The 8.4/10 value-for-money score was measured at the current, below-market price. It says little about how guests will feel at £165, and the score may fall as the price gap closes.

**2. The revenue figure is inconsistent and mislabelled (Sections 2, 5, 7)**
- The context says 112 rooms, but the calculation uses 124. The 124 figure reproduces £204k (124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ £203,800). With 112 rooms it is about **£184,000**.
- The recommendation says "at least £204,000". The figure assumes zero demand response, so it is a best case, not a floor. Calling it "prudent" is the reverse of the truth.
- The calculation treats every occupied room as paying BAR. Corporate, group, contracted and discounted rates, OTA commission and VAT (if £145 is VAT-inclusive) all reduce the real uplift. Please state whether the figure is net or gross.
- Rooms booked before 15 May for stays after 1 June stay at £145, so year-one revenue will be lower, especially in June to August.
- Friday and Saturday are pooled. With 31 Saturday sell-outs, Saturday is probably near capacity and Friday is probably much softer. A single average hides where the risk is.

**3. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business (Section 4)**
- Weddings account for about 38% of Saturday room bookings, and those guests arrive Saturday and leave Sunday. A two-night minimum hits the largest Saturday segment directly. The only protection is for group rates "already contracted", which doesn't cover future weddings.
- The document doesn't say whether wedding blocks will be exempt, or what happens if couples and guests go elsewhere.
- On nights that already sell out, a minimum stay can only displace demand, because those single-night guests are already filling the rooms. The benefit depends on guests extending their stay rather than leaving, which is not evidenced.
- The Friday and Sunday gain is "not quantified but material". That is an assertion. Sunday occupancy isn't shown anywhere.

## Smaller points
- **Break-even is missing.** The rise pays for itself unless occupancy falls from 79% to about 69%, a drop of roughly 10 points. That is useful context, and the proposal should show it alongside scenarios of 0, -3, -5 and -8 points.
- **The monitoring trigger is weak.** It is a "review" only, and it is judged against 2025 rather than the market. By the time a monthly report shows a shortfall, the season is gone. Add pace/pick-up thresholds and a named decision-maker.
- **Ancillary revenue is ignored.** Lost occupancy also means lost F&B and spa income.
- **The competitor comparison is incomplete.** Rate gaps don't show whether competitors fill at £165 to £180. Their occupancy or RevPAR would be better evidence.
- **"Recovered strongly since 2023"** has no data behind it.
- **Notice period.** 15 May to 1 June is about 2.5 weeks, which is short for summer inventory on OTAs.

## Suggested changes
1. Fix the room count and restate revenue on realised ADR, with downside scenarios.
2. Replace the July comparison with a year-on-year or comp-set comparison, or soften the claim to "no evidence of sensitivity at a £10 rise".
3. Consider differentiated pricing, such as a larger rise on sell-out Saturdays and a smaller one on Fridays.
4. Exempt wedding blocks from the minimum stay, or quantify the risk, and apply the minimum only on peak or high-demand Saturdays.
5. Quantify the two-night minimum or present it as a trial.
6. Make the monitoring trigger actionable.

**A note on timing:** the document is dated April 2026 with a 1 June 2026 start. If the change went ahead, there is now several months of real data that would answer most of these questions. It would be worth checking the actual results against the assumptions.
